newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition keeps up street protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition keeps up street protests.

text.p: Thousands of Serbian opposition supporters took to the streets on Thursday to demand authorities recognise the results of local elections.
Some 20,000 people marched to the Serbian parliament building in the capital Belgrade, chanting against President Slobodan Milosevic and the ruling Socialists.
It was the fourth day of protests in Belgrade and other towns since the opposition claimed victory in run-off municipal elections held on Sunday.

Zoran Djindjic, one of three opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, said authorities were committing extensive fraud to overturn the vote and said demonstrations would continue until the Socialists verified poll results.
"We will protest every day until we secure this right," Djindjic told independent Belgrade radio B-92.
Authorities sent police with riot gear to protect parliament and town halls in several towns but no clashes were reported.
Electoral officials on Tuesday confirmed the opposition's victory in the capital Belgrade, an unprecedented defeat for the Milosevic's Socialists.
But authorities failed to announce final results in other towns where Zajedno said it also scored clear majorities.
Electoral commissions controlled by the Socialists have cited unspecified irregularities in municipalities where the opposition said it won, and ordered another round of voting.
Opposition leaders said they would remain inside the parliament until the government or courts responded.

Opposition leaders were unable to speak to the crowd because police allegedly seized sound equipment and blocked exits. Organisers had to lower a string from the fifth floor window and pull up a megaphone so opposition leaders could be heard.
"They have our sound equipment but we have Belgrade!" Djindjic said, prompting a roar from the crowd.

"We are demanding that authorities recognise the electoral will of the citizens," said Djindjic, expected to take over as mayor of Belgrade. He said it was time democratic reforms that swept through the rest of Eastern Europe spread to Serbia.

The Socialist party responded for the first time on Thursday. Spokesman Ivica Dacic said the Zajedno coalition "prematurely" declared it won in several towns and said results would be announced at the end of the "electoral procedure".
He also accused the wife of opposition leader Vuk Draskovic of inciting violence in comments to reporters on Wednesday.
State television has not shown footage of the demonstrations but the state Tanjug news agency blasted the opposition.

"Are they afraid of the results of the (electoral procedure), or are they afraid of the responsibility which power brings, or are they accustomed to the role of those whose only goal is to sow chaos and confusion?" it said.
Zajedno officials alleged Socialist party members had "stolen" election material from polling stations in the southern town of Nis, where the opposition says it won a majority.
Several thousand people gathered in the centre of Nis on Thursday and organisers said university students and factory workers had launched strikes in support of the opposition.
A leftist coalition including the Socialists won federal elections earlier this month after a state media campaign portrayed Milosevic as a peacemaker.
But in the run-off for municipal elections on Sunday, the Socialists lost badly in the country's major industrial centres.
It was a setback for Milosevic, but the former communist party leader retains supreme authority in a country which human rights workers describe as an authoritarian police state.
